あまり (amari) limits the extent of ability, making the sentence sound less confident. · In Japanese culture, you are expected to downplay any ablitlies you may have. If people compliment you, you must refuse the compliment and say that it's not true. Someone who is confident comes off as arrogent to Japanese people.

すみません、 今[いま]は ちょっと。。。
Sorry, not right now…
Travel

すみません (sumimasen) means "excuse me" or "sorry." 今 (ima) means "now," and は (wa) is the topic marker. ちょっと (chotto) means "a little" or "a bit," but in this context, it can be used to indicate hesitation or politely decline something. The phrase can be completed depending on the situation, such as "Sorry, not right now, maybe later" or "Sorry, it's a bit difficult right now." It's often used when politely refusing an offer or request. · Direct refusals are seen as rude and too direct, so many Japanese speakers will use a trailing response instead of a direct no.
マクドナルドに 行[い]きたいんですが

Travel
Same structure as the previous phrase, with マクドナルド (Makudo narudo) referring to McDonald's, and the verb 行きたいんですが (ikitain desu ga) showing the speaker's desire to go.

IC カードは どこで 買[か]えますか？

"ICカード" refers to the IC card, and "は" is the topic particle, indicating that the sentence is about the IC card. "どこで" means "where" in the context of location, with "で" marking where the action happens. "買えますか" is the potential form of "買う" (to buy), asking if it's possible to buy the card. · IC cards are pre-paid cards used to purchase train tickets and can also be used at many vending machines or convenience stores. You can order one online before you arrive in Japan and pick it up at the airport. The most popular amoung tourists is the Welcome Suica card.
